article_title: The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces
citation: Benjamin Paaßen, Barbara Hammer, Thomas W. Price, Tiffany Barnes, Sebastian Gross, Niels Pinkwart. (2018). The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 10, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org
title: Use bottom-out edit hints because principle-based hints are skipped and edit hints reveal only a small part of the solution
description: The article argues for focusing on edit-based bottom-out hints despite pedagogical concerns. Edit hints "display only a very small part of the solution (a single edit), allowing the student to finish most of the problem themselves", and students who game the system "simply skip through such hints to reach the bottom-out hint", so principle-based hints do not prevent hint abuse. More elaborate hint strategies are often unavailable because expert-crafted hint messages are difficult to apply at scale.
requirements: Edit hints should be judged relevant and interpretable, as a study by Price et al. (2017b) indicates for human tutors
constraints: Revealing the next step deprives students of finding it themselves; the article suggests displaying such hints only as a last resort after principle-based hints
target_learners: students requesting help in intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: continuing independent work after receiving a hint
examples: The article cites Aleven et al. (2016) and Shih et al. (2008) on hint reflection and sense-making

article_title: From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee
citation: Jacobs, B., Babineau, K., Parker, D. (2024). From Childcare to Educare: Inspiring Change in Early Childhood Education for Rural Tennessee. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/222
title: Boeren's Lifelong Learning Participation Model as a framework for adult learners' education participation
description: The article's primary guiding framework holds that 'participation in lifelong learning is determined by a number of nested and layered structural factors at the micro, meso, and macro levels.' The micro level covers individual behavioral and social characteristics such as motivation, confidence, race, gender, and geographic location; the meso level covers structures of education and training providers such as courses, class times, and online availability; the macro level covers state and country-level political and cultural climates. The study operationalizes the model by collecting data from service providers (micro) and TECTA administrators (meso) and interpreting findings against Tennessee and U.S. policy contexts (macro).
requirements: Data collection instruments must address all three levels; the study's research questions and interview schedules 'directly address aspects of these levels' to capture relationships among them.
target_learners: adult early childhood education providers, particularly rural learners and women of color
target_learning_goals: participation, persistence, and credential attainment in further education (CDA, associate, and bachelor's degrees)
examples: The study collected data from both service providers (micro level) and TECTA administrators (meso level) and presented findings considering the political and cultural realities of Tennessee and the United States (macro level).

article_title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
citation: Jiawen Tao, Miao Peng, Yaoming Li, Xiaokun Yuan, Mengzhou Wu, Wenhan Yu, Guoan Wang, Nuo Chen, Tong Yang, Maxm Pan. (2026). Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109
title: Treat book-level organization as a first-class axis in synthetic pre-training data design, in both construction and training-time packaging
description: The article argues that how synthetic content is organized into coherent books matters beyond the content itself or local rewriting style. On the generation side, a book-level plan provides the scaffold for long, structured text; on the training side, preserving that structure keeps planned adjacent sections in a shared document with continuous positions and shared intra-document attention. The authors state that "organizing related content into coherent books consistently outperforms the alternatives," positioning organization as a first-class data-design axis alongside content and style.
requirements: A retrieval-grounded synthesis pipeline with clustering, hierarchical TOC planning, and book assembly, plus sequence packing with intra-document attention masking at training time
constraints: Each condition is trained once, so training-run variance remains unmeasured; the effect is demonstrated in mid-training settings with an 8% book slice and was not optimized for synthetic-data proportion
target_learners: language models undergoing mid-training or continued pre-training
target_learning_goals: improved downstream knowledge, reasoning, STEM, and code performance
examples: The Full condition retains each TOC-planned textbook as one training document; Split, RandomConcat, and Rephrase controls isolate packaging, length, and rewriting respectively

article_title: Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios
citation: Leman Figen Gül, Burak Delikanlı, Oğulcan Üneşi, Ertuğrul Ömer Gül. (2025). Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios. ITU A|Z • Vol 22 No 3 • November 2025 • 751-774. https://doi.org/10.58278/0.2025.109
title: Boden's three types of creativity as a framework for GenAI-supported design creativity
description: The article adopts Boden's account of creativity in AI as "the ability to generate novel and valuable ideas" and her three ways new ideas arise: "combinational" creativity generating novel combinations of familiar ideas, "exploratory" creativity delving into overlooked potential of conceptual spaces, and "transformational" creativity transforming dimensions of a conceptual space to generate previously impossible structures. The authors use this triad to interpret students' GenAI-supported design processes in the studios, observing the discovery process as exploring the unknown problem space and a combinatorial analogue as solution space enhancement.
requirements: The framework is used interpretively to map observed student design processes onto creativity types
constraints: The article states Boden's triad was observed "to a certain degree" in the students' processes
target_learning_goals: understanding creativity in AI-assisted design processes
examples: The authors mapped students' use of GenAI for early-phase concept development and inspiration to Boden's exploratory creativity, designated as exploring the unknown problem space

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Box 1 quick tests for distinguishing support from substitution
description: Box 1 operationalises the support–substitution distinction with working definitions, quick tests, and illustrative edge cases. Permitted language support is defined as surface-level interventions improving readability 'without adding ideas, sources, or analytical structure'; substitution is defined as interventions creating or materially reshaping the substantive content. The quick tests ask whether an interaction would produce a new idea, a new source, or a re-ordering of analysis, functioning as a shared discretion-discipline device for markers.
requirements: Institutions adopting the framework should expand the edge-case list iteratively as practice generates new grey zones
constraints: The tests are deliberately conservative; where uncertainty remains, the focus should shift to learning traces and the student's ability to explain reasoning steps
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Ex ante clarity about permitted and prohibited GenAI functions for a specific task
examples: Edge cases include sentence-level clarity edits that preserve meaning (support) versus paragraph-level re-composition that changes emphasis (substitution)
key_sources: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Box 3 decision rubric for integrity decision-makers
description: Box 3 provides a standardised rubric guiding integrity decisions: acceptable evidence types (staged submissions, drafts, student explanation of process, verifiable source trail, viva-style checks), weak proxies that should not be determinative (polished language, sudden fluency, non-native phrasing, single detection scores), the decision question on the balance of probabilities, proportionality mapping, and reasons and reviewability requirements. It is designed to 'discipline discretion, improve consistency across markers and faculties, and support reviewability in appeals'.
requirements: Decisions must record reasons linked to the construct and the communicated boundary
Students must have a meaningful opportunity to respond
constraints: Detection outputs may be used only as triage prompts, not as determinative evidence
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Consistent, reviewable, proportionate integrity decision-making under evidentiary uncertainty
examples: Proportionality mapping: educative response for non-disclosure of permitted support; mark-level penalties where institutional notice was ambiguous; escalation for repeated or deliberate substitution

article_title: Human-Centered Design of LLM-Powered Educational Chatbots: A Study with Secondary Teachers
citation: Reichert, H., Briceno, D., Tabarsi, B., Barnes, T. (2026). Human-Centered Design of LLM-Powered Educational Chatbots: A Study with Secondary Teachers. In: Degen, H., Ntoa, S. (eds) Artificial Intelligence in HCI. HCII 2026. LNCS vol 16746. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-31048-4_32
title: Bounded authority model for teacher–AI authority distribution
description: The bounded authority model describes how teachers distribute authority between themselves and AI systems interacting with students. It has two dimensions: authority boundaries, where "teachers retain ultimate control because professional responsibility cannot be delegated", and expertise boundaries, where "AI lacks teachers’ contextual knowledge of students, classrooms, and institutions". The article states this model "operationalizes bounded authority" through protective layers and extends beyond education to other high-stakes professional domains.
requirements: AI systems operate under human supervision rather than autonomously
constraints: Derived from a qualitative study with six secondary teachers in education contexts
target_learning_goals: safe and appropriate use of LLM-powered chatbots in teacher-supervised learning activities
examples: Teachers in the study designed chatbots with domain boundaries restricting scope, content filtering, and teacher override mechanisms

article_title: Learning with pedagogical agents in extended reality: A conceptual research-based framework of agent-centered learning in immersive media environments (ACLIME)
citation: Ross, M., & Kaspar, K. (2025). Learning with pedagogical agents in extended reality: A conceptual research-based framework of agent-centered learning in immersive media environments (ACLIME). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5092-6798
title: Body avatarization continuum: levels of learner representation from real body to full avatar
description: The review adopts Genay et al. (2022)'s body avatarization continuum to describe learner representation in immersive media. Virtualization ranges "from representation through the real body to a completely virtual representation through an avatar," with two interim levels: body accessorization (adding virtual elements such as virtual clothing or digital eyeglasses to a real body) and partial avatarization (partially modifying the body, e.g., changing skin color or adding a third hand). Full avatarization is possible in all immersive formats (VR, AV, and AR), whereas real body representation, body accessorization, and partial avatarization require see-through head-mounted displays and can be implemented only in AV and AR.
requirements: Real body representation, body accessorization, and partial avatarization require head-mounted displays with see-through function
constraints: Full avatarization is possible in all immersive formats; the other forms only in AV and AR
target_learners: learners in AR, AV, and VR learning environments
target_learning_goals: virtual self-experience, self-presence, and embodiment during immersive learning
key_sources: Ross, M., & Kaspar, K. (2025). Learning with pedagogical agents in extended reality: A conceptual research-based framework of agent-centered learning in immersive media environments (ACLIME). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5092-6798

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model: mastery/growth versus well-being pathways
description: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model describes how student appraisals determine which goal pathway activates during learning. The review states the model "described two parallel processing modes: (a) a mastery or learning mode and (b) a coping or well-being mode." When students perceive a task as threatening, negative cognitions and emotions trigger well-being protection; when the task fits their goals, positive cognitions trigger the mastery/growth pathway. The model assigns three purposes to self-regulation: expanding knowledge and skills, preventing threat to the self, and protecting commitments by re-routing attention from the well-being to the mastery pathway.
requirements: Student appraisals of the task determine which pathway is activated
constraints: Students who start in the mastery/growth pathway may switch to the well-being pathway if they detect cues they might not be successful
target_learners: students in secondary and vocational education
examples: Boekaerts developed the On-line Motivation Questionnaire to measure task-specific feelings, thoughts and effort before and after tasks
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model: mastery/growth and well-being pathways
description: Boekaerts' Dual Processing model describes two parallel processing modes in SRL: a mastery or learning mode and a coping or well-being mode. The review explains that "the appraisals made by the students are crucial to determine which goal pathway the students will activate": threatening appraisals trigger negative cognitions and emotions and a well-being pathway, while congruent appraisals trigger positive cognitions and a mastery/growth pathway. The model names three purposes of self-regulation (expanding knowledge and skills, preventing threat to the self, protecting commitments) and gives emotions a key role, with volitional and emotion regulation strategies as bottom-up strategies.
requirements: Student appraisals of the task determine which pathway is activated, so appraisal-sensitive situations are needed to observe the model's dynamics
constraints: Students who start in the mastery/growth pathway may switch to the well-being pathway if they detect cues they might not be successful
target_learners: students in primary, secondary and vocational education
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in learning tasks and emotion regulation during learning
examples: Boekaerts developed the On-line Motivation Questionnaire to measure task-specific feelings, thoughts and effort before and after tasks

article_title: Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills
citation: Davidse, N. J., de Jong, M. T., Bus, A. G., Huijbregts, S. C. J., & Swaab, H. (2010). Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills. Read Writ 24, 395–412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-010-9233-3
title: Book-cover recognition test as a proximal measure of children's book exposure
description: A child-completed test in which children are shown covers of 41 familiar Dutch picture storybooks and asked who the characters are, what the story is called, and what it is about; coders judge whether the child is acquainted with the book, excluding mere knowledge of merchandised characters. The article presents it as "a new instrument—the book-cover recognition test—as a proximal measure of children's book exposure in research and individual assessments of children's literacy environment". In this study it mediated the HLE–literacy relationship and outperformed questionnaire-based HLE measures.
requirements: Picture books selected from top sales and library lending lists so items vary in familiarity
Coding that distinguishes genuine story knowledge from merchandising-based character recognition
constraints: Alpha reliability was .67 in this study
Stainthorp (1997) warned title-recognition scores can be inflated when books are serialized on television
target_learning_goals: Assessing children's book exposure as a predictor of vocabulary and letter knowledge
examples: Children recognized on average 2.68 (SD = 2.34) of 41 book covers; intercoder reliability for the test was .78

article_title: Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills
citation: Davidse, N. J., de Jong, M. T., Bus, A. G., Huijbregts, S. C. J., & Swaab, H. (2010). Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills. Read Writ 24, 395–412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-010-9233-3
title: Share books with all preschool children regardless of their cognitive control skills
description: The study's implication is that book sharing benefits young children across the cognitive control spectrum: "The results also support the hypothesis that book sharing is beneﬁcial for all children. So far, there is no evidence for the hypothesis that effects of book exposure depend on child characteristics such as cognitive control skills." Educators and parents therefore need not gate shared-reading opportunities on children's short-term memory, inhibition, or sustained attention in the preschool years.
requirements: Book exposure opportunities in the preschool period (home, daycare, preschool, or library settings)
constraints: Evidence is correlational; causality cannot be concluded
Tested only in a homogeneous low-to-middle SES native Dutch sample; moderation may emerge in less homogeneous groups or when children practice independently (e.g., from Grade 1)
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary growth and early code-related (letter) knowledge
examples: In the study, children below and above the median on cognitive control measures benefited equally from book exposure as indicated by the book-cover recognition test

article_title: Everyday experiences of memory problems and control: the adaptive role of selective optimization with compensation in the context of memory decline
citation: Hahn Elizabeth A. Ph.D., Lachman Margie E. Ph.D. (2014). Everyday Experiences of Memory Problems and Control: The Adaptive Role of Selective Optimization with Compensation in the Context of Memory Decline. Neuropsychology, development, and cognition. Section B, Aging, neuropsychology and cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4156931/
title: 12-week weekly paper-and-pencil diary protocol for everyday memory problems and perceived control
description: The BOLOS Time 2 battery included a 12-week diary study in which participants completed a weekly report of everyday experiences at the end of each week. The diaries included questions related to "everyday memory problems, perceived control, and a range of health and well-being measures." Everyday memory problems were assessed with 11 items reporting how many days (0-7) each problem occurred, summed to a weekly composite ranging from 0 to 77. Weekly perceived control was a single item asking how much participants felt "in control of my life" that week (1-5). Participants completed the paper-and-pencil diary at home and mailed it back within 24 hours.
requirements: Participants must complete at least two weeks of diaries with complete Time 1 and Time 2 data for inclusion.
constraints: There was a significant drop-off in reports of memory problems over the 12 weeks, so time was included as a covariate; participant burden may result in a drop-off in reports.
target_learning_goals: Assessing naturally-occurring everyday memory problems and weekly fluctuations in perceived control
examples: The current study includes the 103 participants who completed at least two weeks of diaries and had complete data for Time 1 and Time 2.

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x
title: Boston Naming Test (BNT) as a measure of expressive vocabulary for adult struggling readers
description: The Boston Naming Test (Kaplan et al., 2001) is a 60-item confrontation naming test in which participants name line drawings of common objects presented in order of increasing difficulty, with stimulus and phonemic cues given after incorrect answers. It "has been normed on participants ages five through 79" but, as the authors note, "the BNT has not been normed on adult struggling readers and, therefore, may not be an accurate measure of their expressive vocabulary." In this study testing began at item 1 rather than the adult-recommended item 30 because prior research indicated object-naming difficulty in this population.
requirements: Administration decisions must account for the population's known object-naming difficulty; this study began at item 1 instead of the recommended item 30 for adults.
constraints: The BNT has not been normed on adult struggling readers, so results may underestimate relationships with reading skills.
target_learners: Adult struggling readers reading at third- to fifth-grade levels
examples: Administered individually to 232 adult literacy students; mean total correct was 36 (SD = 7.29), and performance on items 1–30 was worse than the Tombaugh and Hubley (1997) normative sample.

article_title: Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers’ instructional patterns in simulation-based training
citation: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x
title: Design simulation-based VET instruction to deliberately maintain and bridge the boundary between simulated and authentic work environments.
description: The article argues that the instructional work of the VET teacher deals with making sense of how simulated and authentic practices are entangled, and with "making choices that imply unravelling such entanglements and keeping the worlds apart to put them back together again". Boundary-work is described as even more emphasized in simulation-based training than in other vocational subjects because of the elements of fidelity and authenticity. Teachers and students must discern what is (ir)relevant to connect or separate the simulated activity from the authentic work practice, handled in the moment-by-moment interaction.
requirements: VET teachers with dual identity as both teachers and professional experts in the vocational field, whose previous professional experiences are constantly present in the simulator-centre.
constraints: The article notes that simulation as an instructional tool alone is not enough for the development of complex skills where learners have different levels of prior knowledge.
target_learners: Upper-secondary VET students in the Natural Resource Program
target_learning_goals: Development of vocational knowledge and skills connecting simulator-based training to future work-related activities
examples: The article illustrates this with a student who orients towards a teacher's instruction about grappling logs on uneven ground even while performing a simplified box-moving task in the simulator.

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Treat boundary conditions as theory-sharpening qualifications, not immutable prescriptions
description: Mayer argues that research-based principles such as the modality principle carry boundary conditions—qualifications like pacing and learner versus system control—and that discovering them helps verify and sharpen theory. On the practical level, "research-based principles such as the modality principle should be implemented in ways that are consistent with the underlying theory rather than being seen as immutable prescriptions that must be followed in all situations". This turns apparent inconsistencies in findings into practical guidance.
requirements: Implementers need knowledge of the underlying theory to judge when a principle applies
constraints: The principle does not apply uniformly in all situations; the modality effect is not found in all studies
target_learners: instructional designers applying multimedia learning principles
target_learning_goals: effective application of multimedia design principles
examples: Mayer cites the modality principle's strongest effects under fast-paced, system-controlled presentation as an observed boundary condition

article_title: Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study
citation: Katharina Luisa Boehme, Thomas Goetz, Markus Feuchter, Franzis Preckel. (2025). Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09991-5
title: Boredom and lack of interest as distinct constructs with different emotional and motivational consequences
description: The article's conceptual framework holds that although boredom and interest overlap phenomenologically, boredom is not the absence of interest. Lack of interest is affectively neutral, whereas boredom is an unpleasant, aversive state with low arousal that provokes avoidance motivation and the wish to escape the situation; lack of interest implies only an absence of approach motivation. The framework also holds that academic boredom and interest are domain-specific and that boredom arises from interactions of task, person (value and perceived control), and environment characteristics, whereas interest is object-specific. The study's CFA and cross-lagged results are presented as empirical support for this separability.
requirements: Measurement models must establish at least metric longitudinal measurement invariance before interpreting stability and cross-lagged path coefficients, and scalar invariance for comparing latent means
constraints: The empirical evidence comes from upper-track German Gymnasium students in mathematics and German only; the article notes limited evidence of between-domain predictive patterns except in grade 5
target_learners: secondary school students in upper-track German Gymnasium, grades 5–8
target_learning_goals: students' academic emotions and motivational development in mathematics and German
examples: The study operationalised boredom with two AEQ-M items and interest with a three-item PALMA scale, rated on 5-point Likert scales, across four waves
key_sources: Katharina Luisa Boehme, Thomas Goetz, Markus Feuchter, Franzis Preckel. (2025). Is Boredom the Opposite of Interest? A Longitudinal Reciprocal Effect Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09991-5

article_title: Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial
citation: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946
title: Include board-game play in primary classrooms as an alternative or complement to regular direct instruction for cognitive and academic development
description: The article concludes that classroom time spent playing modern board games can serve cognitive and educational development at least as well as regular teaching. Based on the trial results, it states that "the inclusion of board games in the classroom could favour the development of executive functions in primary school children just as much as, or even better than, regular classes", and that commercial games designed to entertain nevertheless led to reading and maths benefits. The recommendation is grounded in the trial's measured group-time effects rather than in motivation ratings, which were not collected.
requirements: Games selected for the executive functions and curricular competencies they can train, with sessions organised by a programme manual
constraints: The direction of transfer from executive-function training to academic skills was not tested; inhibition and flexibility gains did not favour the play group in grades two to six
target_learners: primary school students from first to sixth grade
examples: In the cluster-randomised trial, the experimental group played commercial board games in class for 12 one-hour sessions over six weeks while the active control group followed regular classes
key_sources: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Cultivate a desired emotion or disposition by voluntarily performing its outward bodily manifestations
description: A method of emotional control, described as an outgrowth of the James-Lange theory though acted on earlier: assume the bodily attitude characteristic of an emotion to further its development. James states that 'when we wish to cultivate a certain disposition, we should go through with the movements which make up the outward manifestation of that disposition'. Thorndike and Münsterberg endorse the same principle, the latter treating feelings as essentially motor reactions controllable through voluntary movement.
requirements: The learner must voluntarily assume the movements and attitudes that make up the outward manifestation of the desired emotion or disposition
constraints: The article states it is impossible to say to just what extent one can control his emotions and feelings by assuming appropriate bodily attitudes, while affirming there must be something in the principle
target_learning_goals: cultivation of desired emotional dispositions such as courage, cheerfulness, and affection
examples: Thorndike's illustrations: a frightened person walking steadily toward the enemy, shouting defiance and brandishing his weapon so fear may be replaced by courage; and a kindergarten teacher treating a disfigured baby with lap, smiles and caresses until disgust gives way to tolerance and even affection.
key_sources: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/

article_title: Needed research in method.
citation: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl
title: Book's Psychology of Skill as a model of experimental research in method
description: The article holds up W. F. Book's monograph as an exemplar of the fourth class of method work, where emphasis is placed on the child's mind working through a curriculum element. The article describes it as "an experimental study of habit-formation as exemplified in typewriting," studying specific habits and general aspects of mental life such as merging of smaller habits, fatigue, mental inertia, warming up, and kinds of practice that counted most for efficiency. The author argues such work shows the crucial points in a learning process and yields vital, definite suggestions for teachers.
requirements: Experimental study of a concrete learning task within the curriculum
constraints: The article cites it as an example from the psychological laboratory, not as research done in classrooms
target_learning_goals: studying habit formation and skill acquisition
key_sources: Clayton C. Kohl. (1911). Needed Research in Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Needed+Research+in+Method%22+Kohl

article_title: Communications and discussions. The conference on mental hygiene at Boston.
citation: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: The Boston Mental Hygiene Conference and its accompanying exhibit
description: A Mental Hygiene Conference was "held in Boston, March 31 to April 4, inclusive, conducted by the National Committee for Mental Hygiene and the newly formed Massachusetts Society for Mental Hygiene." In connection with it was an exhibit similar to those given at earlier hygiene congresses. The program included addresses by Dr. Paton, President-Emeritus Eliot, Dr. Putnam, President G. Stanley Hall, and other medical and institutional speakers, plus an elaborate printed program of facts and practical suggestions.
requirements: Organization by a national committee and a newly formed state society, with speakers and an accompanying exhibit
constraints: A one-time 1913 event; the article gives no evaluation of the conference's effects
target_learners: the general public addressed by the conference program
examples: The closing session included Dr. Putnam on "Our Obligation to Understand the Working of Our Own Minds" and President G. Stanley Hall on "Mind and Food."

article_title: Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System
citation: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0
title: Grant learners bounded exploration in embedded tutors, guiding them back on path quickly and blocking only unrelated actions
description: When tutoring on an existing interface, the article recommends a "middle-of-the-road" approach: learners keep freedom to explore, since exploration "is a natural part of learning", but are guided back on path as quickly as possible and blocked when necessary. In the Paint.NET tutor, users could explore drop menus a limited number of times, feedback was planned for plausible related errors, and unrelated menu items were blocked with a reminder of the current goal.
requirements: The tutor must detect which learner actions are related versus unrelated to the current goal
Movable hint windows so feedback does not obscure needed interface parts
constraints: More flexibility generally equates to more complicated tutors; Paint.NET students reported the system allowed too much freedom to explore
target_learners: novice learners using authentic software applications
target_learning_goals: staying on the solution path while retaining exploratory freedom in the target application
examples: Paint.NET tutor allowed 7–10 menu explorations, gave feedback on plausible related errors, and blocked unrelated menu items with a goal reminder
key_sources: Stephen B. Gilbert, Stephen B. Blessing, Enruo Guo. (2015). Authoring Effective Embedded Tutors: An Overview of the Extensible Problem Specific Tutor (xPST) System. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:428–454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0045-0

article_title: Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback
citation: Istenič, A. (2021). Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 117–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09955-w
title: Borup, West, and Thomas (2015) study on text versus video communication for instructor feedback
description: A mixed-method research study comparing video feedback and text-based feedback in a blended learning course through the perceptions of student teachers and teacher educators. The study critically analyzed feedback "from the perspective of media richness theory" and identified "three elements: content and utility, timing and efficiency, and delivery and affective support". It examined how asynchronous text feedback capitalizes on asynchronous text communication and adds characteristics of verbal and non-verbal cues.
requirements: Blended learning course context with student teachers and teacher educators

article_title: Exploring the role of synchrony in asynchronous, synchronous, and quasi-synchronous online learner engagement
citation: Duncan Culbreth · Florence Martin. (2025). Exploring the role of synchrony in asynchronous, synchronous, and quasi-synchronous online learner engagement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10504-y
title: Bichronous online learning framework extended to position MIM quasi-synchronicity as supporting BOL
description: Bichronous online learning (BOL) is "a framework that considers synchrony as a spectrum with three categories: Asynchronous, synchronous, and bichronous", blending asynchronous and synchronous modalities within one learning environment. This study extends BOL by framing mobile instant messaging (MIM) as a quasi-synchronous modality, and proposes that "quasi-synchronicity may be considered a subset of BOL", since a single service can support a range of synchronies through secondary features.
requirements: A modality must demonstrate both asynchronous and synchronous qualities, as MIM does via notifications allowing students to read messages after posting
constraints: Research on instructional design for BOL is described as nascent
The proposition rests on one course-based mixed-method study
target_learners: graduate and upperclassman undergraduate students in online courses
examples: Debates in an online graduate course were run via Moodle forum, Zoom video call, and Discord MIM across three consecutive weeks, with one student describing MIM as striking "a nice middle ground between the forum (almost completely asynchronous) and the zoom call (almost completely synchronous)"
key_sources: Duncan Culbreth · Florence Martin. (2025). Exploring the role of synchrony in asynchronous, synchronous, and quasi-synchronous online learner engagement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10504-y

article_title: “How Did I Do?”: Giving learners effective and affective feedback
citation: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2
title: Borup et al.'s (2015) blended-course feedback study as an anchor for future feedback research and practice
description: The article treats Borup et al.'s (2015) study of teacher candidate and instructor feedback perceptions in blended learning as a foundational reference point, calling it "a critical anchor to support future efforts". The study, published in Educational Technology Research and Development, is used to ground the commentary's strategies and design goals for digital feedback experiences.
requirements: Serves as a grounding reference for efforts to improve feedback experiences in digital learning spaces.
target_learning_goals: improved feedback experiences in blended and online learning
examples: The commentary builds its feedback delivery strategies for educators directly on this study.

article_title: Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies.
citation: Li Shuze, Wei Wei, Li Xiaofeng, Ma Li, Li Qiujuan, Sun Xiance, Chen Xin. (2024). Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05917-x
title: BOPPPS six-step teaching model
description: BOPPPS is a goal-oriented, student-centered teaching model divided into "six essential steps: bridge-in, objective, pre-assessment, participatory learning, and summary" (with post-assessment), originating from Canadian teacher skill training put forward by Douglas Kerrin in 1978. In the blended version, teachers use an online platform for pre-class introduction resources, online pre-tests of 10–20 exercises, in-class or online participatory discussions, group reporting and role-playing, post-testing, and in-class plus post-class summarization. The article treats the six stages as "a coherent, systematic, and actionable teaching design model" and evaluates its blended implementation against LBL.
requirements: An online teaching platform (e.g. Xuexi Tong, Rain Classes, MOOC) to deliver pre-class resources, tests, and discussions
Teachers able to evaluate and modify each of the six steps, which the article says makes it extremely convenient to implement
constraints: The article notes some students still reported poor classroom interaction in purely online courses, which the blended mode is said to compensate for
target_learners: Chinese medical undergraduate students in higher medical education
examples: In the pre-test phase teachers generate 10–20 exercises aligned with teaching objectives online; applied knowledge is taught through role-playing involving both students and teachers
key_sources: Li Shuze, Wei Wei, Li Xiaofeng, Ma Li, Li Qiujuan, Sun Xiance, Chen Xin. (2024). Impacts of blended learning with BOPPPS model on Chinese medical undergraduate students: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 studies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05917-x

article_title: Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning
citation: Motlagh, S. F. P., & Nasab, M. S. B. (2015). Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.227
title: Bold target vocabulary words in meaning-oriented texts to foster L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article recommends that teachers presenting new vocabulary in texts typographically enhance the target words, with bolding as the preferred device. It states that "instructing new vocabulary accompanied by bolding target words will lead to statistically more effective learning of vocabulary", and that input enhancement lets students overcome vocabulary comprehension problems while teachers work out solutions for understanding target vocabulary in texts. The recommendation is grounded in the study's finding that the bolding group achieved the highest vocabulary means and significantly outperformed the other enhancement conditions.
requirements: Target words must be embedded in texts used within meaning-oriented instruction; learners should not be told they are being evaluated on vocabulary, as in the study
constraints: Evidence comes from a small, single-sex (male), upper-intermediate sample at one institute; the article states there were not as many subjects as ideally needed and that re-examination might yield different outputs
target_learners: upper-intermediate EFL learners in language institute classes
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary knowledge and ability to answer vocabulary questions on target words
examples: Across eight 45-minute sessions, experimental groups read the same two texts with target words bolded, underlined, or capitalized, then answered multiple-choice vocabulary and comprehension questions, while the control group read the unenhanced texts
key_sources: Motlagh, S. F. P., & Nasab, M. S. B. (2015). Assessing Input Enhancement as Positive Factor and Its Impact on L2 Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.227

article_title: Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies
citation: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560
title: Use bootstrapping to test the significance of the indirect effect
description: The article recommends bootstrapping over the joint test of significance for testing the indirect effect: "Bootstrapping (Shrout & Bolger, 2002) is a more reliable approach, and also allows for the estimation of confidence intervals." Bootstrapping resamples with replacement across a large draw of samples (1,000 to 5,000 is common) to create a sampling distribution for ab, with a simple correction for the bias arising because the product of two normal variables is not always normal.
requirements: Modern software packages (Mplus, SAS, Stata, Amos) or the Preacher and Hayes SPSS/SAS macros to perform bootstrapping
constraints: The mean of the bootstrapped distribution will not always equal the indirect effect, which introduces bias absent a correction
target_learners: educational researchers conducting mediation analyses of intervention studies
target_learning_goals: accurate statistical inference about mediated treatment effects
examples: The article notes the joint test of significance is generally considered a preliminary rather than a confirmatory test of the null hypothesis that ab = 0
key_sources: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560

article_title: Drama-Based Science Teaching and Its Effect on Students' Understanding of Scientific Concepts and Their Attitudes towards Science Learning
citation: Osama H. Abed. (2016). Drama-Based Science Teaching and Its Effect on Students' Understanding of Scientific Concepts and Their Attitudes towards Science Learning. International Education Studies, 9(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n10p163
title: Body-as-model physical simulation drama activities for the Heat unit
description: The author designed drama activities in which students' bodies serve as models of atoms and molecules: wrists and elbows act as chemical bonds, and students mime changes in speed, spacing, and bonding as matter moves among solid, liquid, and gas states. Heat transfer is mimed with a red card as the heating source, passed or triggering movement along a queue. The author told students "you are going to be the models of atoms and molecules". Water's negative thermal expansion was deliberately excluded from the activities.
requirements: A classroom space large enough to mark out a virtual ice cube on the floor and let students diffuse across the room
The teacher designs and guides the miming scenes for each state of matter and heat transfer
constraints: Water as an exception (negative thermal expansion) was not discussed in the activities
Activities were designed for one unit (Heat) of the seventh-grade textbook
target_learning_goals: understanding the three states of matter
understanding methods of heat transfer (conduction, radiation, convection)
examples: Students moved very slowly locked elbow-to-elbow inside a floor-marked ice cube for the solid state, moved faster while still linked for liquid, and separated and diffused through the whole classroom for gas
key_sources: Osama H. Abed. (2016). Drama-Based Science Teaching and Its Effect on Students' Understanding of Scientific Concepts and Their Attitudes towards Science Learning. International Education Studies, 9(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n10p163

article_title: The Effect of Video-Based Tasks in Listening Comprehension of Iranian Pre-Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Abdullah Sarani, Esmail Zare Behtash and Saieed Moslemi Nezhad Arani. (2014). The Effect of Video-Based Tasks in Listening Comprehension of Iranian Pre-intermediate EFL Learners. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, No. 8, pp. 29-47. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777
title: Bottom-up and top-down processing frameworks for teaching L2 listening, with metacognitive knowledge split into person, task, and strategy knowledge
description: The article organizes L2 listening instruction around two processing directions. Bottom-up processing "demands an awareness of sounds and words in the stream of speech" and acknowledges "the primacy of the acoustic signal"; top-down processing promotes learners' metacognitive awareness so they can apply strategies independently. Metacognitive knowledge is divided into person knowledge (e.g., anxiety, motivation), task knowledge (purpose, demands, text organization), and strategy knowledge for dealing with listening problems.
requirements: Instruction should give learners a framework and ladder-like situation that builds on prior knowledge so they learn how to listen
constraints: The article notes bottom-up processing is not exactly a method of teaching; Field (2004) treats the terms as directions of processing rather than levels
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension strategy use and metacognitive awareness
examples: The study states it continues Long and Doughty's three-topic framework (cognitive and social dimension, approaches to teaching, assessment of listening)

article_title: Middle School Learners' Use of Latin Roots to Infer the Meaning of Unfamiliar Words
citation: Amy C. Crosson & Margaret G. McKeown. (2016). Middle School Learners' Use of Latin Roots to Infer the Meaning of Unfamiliar Words. Cognition and Instruction, 34(2), 148-171. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2016.1145121
title: Framework for morphological problem solving with bound Latin roots: memory representations, metalinguistic insight, and flexibility
description: The article proposes that using bound Latin roots (e.g., voc in advocate) to infer unfamiliar word meanings requires three constructs building on Schreuder and Baayen's morphological processing model: "established memory representations(i.e., concept nodes)forboundrootsandtheirmeanings," metalinguistic insight about how to use this information for problem solving, and flexibility in applying root meanings—switching among orthographic forms (vid/vis) and fitting root meaning to context rather than bluntly plugging it in. Root accessibility is moderated by semantic transparency, phonological transparency, and orthographic stability and uniqueness.
requirements: Learners need established memory representations for bound roots and their meanings, plus metalinguistic insight into how roots carry information about word meaning
constraints: The article states Schreuder and Baayen's framework is not adequate to explain a learner's use of bound morphemes, since bound roots are not always redundant and transparent enough to activate their own nodes
target_learning_goals: inferring meanings of unfamiliar morphologically complex academic vocabulary
examples: RAVE morphology lessons taught roots such as spect and min with root-related extension words, and taught that spelling and pronunciation of roots can vary and that there are false alarms such as val in value versus valve
key_sources: Amy C. Crosson & Margaret G. McKeown. (2016). Middle School Learners' Use of Latin Roots to Infer the Meaning of Unfamiliar Words. Cognition and Instruction, 34(2), 148-171. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2016.1145121

article_title: Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability
citation: Samira Sehati, Morteza Khodabandehlou. (2017). Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability. Journal of Educational Issues, Vol. 3, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i2.12323
title: Two-process model of listening comprehension: bottom-up (data-driven) and top-down (conceptually-driven) processing
description: The article frames listening as an active process of "deciphering and constructing meaning from both verbal and non-verbal messages" (citing Nunan), rejecting the label of passive skill. It distinguishes two subsuming cognitive processes: bottom-up processing builds meaning from the smallest spoken units up to whole texts, supported by suprasegmental features such as stress, rhythm and intonation, while top-down processing interprets speaker-intended meaning using learners' background knowledge and schemata. The article uses this framework to argue that lack of background knowledge can hamper comprehension, motivating visual supports for listening.
requirements: Learners need practice in both processes, e.g. sound-discrimination activities for bottom-up processing and gist-extraction activities for top-down processing
constraints: The article notes significant lack of background knowledge can hamper learners' comprehension of an utterance
examples: The article cites training activities such as discriminating two sounds or distinguishing rising and falling intonations for bottom-up processing
key_sources: Samira Sehati, Morteza Khodabandehlou. (2017). Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability. Journal of Educational Issues, Vol. 3, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i2.12323

article_title: Using Group Discussion with Taiwan's EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations
citation: Shen, F.-Y. (2013). Using Group Discussion with Taiwan’s EFL College Students: A Comparison of Comprehension Instruction for Book Club, Literature Circles, and Instructional Conversations. English Language Teaching, 6(12), 58-. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n12p58
title: Book Club integrates reading, writing, instruction, and community share into a complete reading program
description: Book Club is a discussion-centered reading instruction approach consisting of four recurring elements. The article describes it as follows: "The Book Club program consisted of four elements: reading, writing, instruction, and community share." After teacher instruction, students write response journals, then convene in peer-led small-group discussions based on their journals, and finally join a whole-class community share to exchange insights about the text. Students generate questions, control turn-taking, and hold interpretive authority.
requirements: Response journals that students use as the basis for peer-led discussion.
A community share phase in which the whole class exchanges insights about the text.
examples: In the study's Book Club lessons, students read independently, wrote response journals, discussed in peer-led groups, and closed with community sharing.

article_title: Influence of Instructional Practices on Secondary School Students' Achievement in Mathematics
citation: Odhiambo marble Nandwa, Dr. Duncan Wekesa Wasike, Professor Toili William Wanjala. (2015). Influence of Instructional Practices on Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.26. https://www.iiste.org/Journals/index.php/JEP/article/view/31336
title: Combining behavioural objectives with peer instruction and concept tests (BO-PICT)
description: BO-PICT integrates Behavioural Objective-Based instruction with Peer Instruction enriched with Concept Tests into a single instructional sequence. The article reports that "E3 that used BO-PICT was superior to the rest of the experimental groups", achieving the highest post-test mean (66.4) and greatest gain (35.3). The pattern combines explicit behavioural objectives with interactive peer discussion and concept-based testing.
requirements: Teachers must be able to state behavioural objectives in lesson notes and facilitate peer instruction with concept tests.
constraints: Tested only on compound proportion and rates of work in form three secondary mathematics over three weeks.
target_learning_goals: achievement in compound proportion and rates of work
examples: Group E3 used both BOB and PICT strategies (BO-PICT) in two randomly selected schools.

article_title: The Boundary Spanner in Professional Development Schools: In Search of Common Nomenclature
citation: Burns, R. W., & Baker, W. (2015). The Boundary Spanner in Professional Development Schools: In Search of Common Nomenclature. School-University Partnerships, 9(2), 28-40. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1097249
title: A three-component conceptual framework for describing boundary-spanning roles in PDSs
description: The authors propose a conceptual framework with three components: Role Identities (home institution and position), Role Characteristics (duration and location), and Role Responsibilities as Supervisory Tasks. The framework is designed to "preserve the contextual speciﬁcities of terminology while simultaneously providing structure to foster common understanding." It emerged from the meta-analysis findings and is intended to guide future research descriptions of boundary-spanning roles.
requirements: Definitions should include descriptors for home institution, position, duration, location, and supervisory tasks
constraints: The four position categories resulted from this study's data; additional positions may exist and more research is needed
target_learning_goals: clearer understanding of PDS partnership roles

article_title: Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study.
citation: Zhu Xiaocheng, Tang Anliu, Chin Munle, Chang Huan. (2026). Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10042-y
title: BOPPPS framework as a structure for guiding purposeful observation in early clinical exposure
description: The Bridge-in, Objectives, Pre-assessment, Participatory learning, Post-assessment, and Summary (BOPPPS) model is a structured, learner-centered instructional framework. In this study it was "not used merely as a general teaching format, but as a structure for guiding novice learners through a complex perioperative environment": Bridge-in and Objectives clarified focus before exposure, Pre-assessment identified baseline understanding, Participatory learning used checklist-guided observation, and Post-assessment and Summary supported reflection.
requirements: Instructor training and collective preparation to standardize teaching objectives, observation scope, and evaluation criteria
A workflow-oriented observation checklist with student and instructor versions to translate clinical processes into observable learning tasks
constraints: Evidence for BOPPPS applied to early anesthesiology clinical exposure was limited before this study
The framework was implemented within a fixed 180-minute clerkship schedule at a single institution
target_learners: Second-year undergraduate medical students in early clinical exposure
target_learning_goals: Understanding anesthesiologists' responsibilities, patient safety, and team collaboration
examples: The structured group received a 20-minute Bridge-in and Objectives session and a 40-minute checklist-based reflection and summary session in place of the conventional 45-minute lecture and 15-minute Q&A
key_sources: Zhu Xiaocheng, Tang Anliu, Chin Munle, Chang Huan. (2026). Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10042-y

citation: Li P, Taoyu J, Yaxin L, Xiao-li P, Muzi L, Haoying D. (2026). Evaluation of the Bridge-in, Objective, Preassessment, Participatory Learning, Postassessment, and Summary–Based Instructional Model in Disaster Nursing: Quasi-Experimental Study. title: BOPPPS model as a structured closed-loop instructional framework with six components organized across three phases
description: The BOPPPS (Bridge-in, Objective, Preassessment, Participatory Learning, Postassessment, and Summary) model is a student-centered, closed-loop instructional framework introduced by Douglas Kerr in 1978. It structures lessons around six components spanning preclass preparation, in-class implementation, and postclass consolidation phases. In this study, the model was implemented through the Chaoxing Learning Platform to deliver blended disaster nursing education, with preassessment and postassessment scores providing timely feedback for adjusting teaching strategies.
requirements: Requires an online learning platform for resource delivery and real-time feedback
Requires structured preclass, in-class, and postclass phases with defined activities for each BOPPPS component
constraints: Originally designed for general lesson structuring; its application to highly specialized fields like disaster nursing was largely absent from domestic Chinese research prior to this study
target_learning_goals: Emergency response principles and first aid skills

article_title: A BOPPPS-PBL Nursing Innovation Course for Newly Recruited Nurses: A Single-Group Quantitative Pilot Evaluation of Creativity, Self-Efficacy and 1-Year Project Outputs.
citation: Yang Hao, Jing Xiaosha, Guan Yujia, Yang Min, Bai Ting, Xing Lingling, Mu Dan, Wang Xihong, Liu Hongqian. (2026). A BOPPPS‐PBL Nursing Innovation Course for Newly Recruited Nurses: A Single‐Group Quantitative Pilot Evaluation of Creativity, Self‐Efficacy and 1‐Year Project Outputs. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70734
title: BOPPPS-PBL integrated teaching model: BOPPPS structure scaffolding PBL within the participatory learning phase
description: The model combines the six-stage BOPPPS sequence (Bridge-in, Objectives, Preassessment, Participatory Learning, Postassessment, Summary) with PBL embedded in the participatory phase as a four-stage cycle of "situational construction, problem exploration through core questions, collaborative solution design and reflective evaluation". BOPPPS provides sequencing, objectives and assessment checkpoints for novice learners, while PBL drives inquiry on real departmental problems. title: The BOPPPS-integrated model (BIM): a modular instructional framework integrating PBL, TBL, and CBL into BOPPPS sessions
description: BIM is a student-centered instructional model that maps PBL, TBL, and CBL onto the six BOPPPS sessions. As the article states, it "systematically integrates PBL and CBL into bridge-in and summary sessions to contextualize learning and reinforce core concepts; PBL into pre-assessment and post-assessment sessions"; and PBL, TBL, and CBL into participatory learning sessions to promote collaboration, knowledge integration, and practical skill development. description: The article recommends bootcamps as "a useful adjunct to the traditional apprenticeship training model, as they provide a standardised and equal approach towards the training of ST3s that can integrate the use of performance metrics unlike the variability of clinical exposure". constraints: The study compared bootcamp only to no prior teaching, with no comparison to other teaching courses; self-reported gains may not translate to clinical proficiency
target_learners: Doctors transitioning into a new specialty role, here ENT ST3 registrars
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of technical and non-technical skills expected at the start of higher specialty training
examples: The study's two-day bootcamp with ten skills sessions covering ward, elective and emergency ENT presentations for 32 registered ST3 trainees

title: BOPPPS six-stage lesson-structure model
description: The BOPPPS model, suggested by the Canadian Instructional Skills Workshop in the 1970s, organizes a lesson into six stages: "course introduction (B-Bridge in), learning objectives or outcomes (O-Objective or Outcome), pre assessment (P-Pre assessment), participatory learning (P-Participant Learning), post assessment (P-Post assessment), and summary (S-Summary)". examples: The lesson on iron deficiency anemia was designed in six BOPPPS modules (Fig. 1; Table 1), with a clinical-case bridge-in, knowledge/ability/quality objectives, pre-assessment questions, participatory learning, post-assessment and summary

article_title: Assessment of the effectiveness of BOPPPS-based hybrid teaching model in physiology education.
citation: Liu Xiao-Yu, Lu Chunmei, Zhu Hui, Wang Xiaoran, Jia Shuwei, Zhang Ying, Wen Haixia, Wang Yu-Feng. (2022). Assessment of the effectiveness of BOPPPS-based hybrid teaching model in physiology education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03269-y
title: BOPPPS: a six-element teaching model for organizing offline lectures
description: BOPPPS is a teaching theory abbreviating Bridge-in, Objectives and Outcomes of Learning, Pre-assessment, Participatory learning, Post-assessment and Summary, first introduced by Douglas Kerr from the University of British Columbia and developed recently in medical education in China. The article describes each element's function: bridge-in draws students' attention to the course contents, objectives give a general understanding of content, pre-assessment challenges students and guides attention to the main lecture, participatory learning stresses a student-centered approach and inspires initiative, post-assessment shows the teacher how well students mastered content, and summary gives students a mind mapping that strengthens memory. The article uses BOPPPS as the offline foundation into which online teaching was incorporated to form HBOPPPS.
requirements: The article states the time limitation of offline teaching restrains BOPPPS's applicability, particularly the methods of pre- and post-assessments and summary
constraints: The article states classical BOPPPS is relatively weak in enriching students' knowledge, establishing feed-forward and feedback connections, targeting general obstacles, and meeting diverse learning style preferences
target_learning_goals: clear organization of the teaching process
examples: In the offline BOPPPS condition, a course contents-associated video or image was presented at bridge-in, single/multiple choice questions were used in the first 5 min for pre-assessment, and group discussions and student presentations constituted participatory learning

title: Body Interact virtual patient simulation platform used for fully online pre-graduation clinical training
description: Body Interact™ is a platform providing education training by means of "virtual patients built with artificial intelligence". Students interview the virtual patient, perform physical examination, order laboratory and imaging tests, administer medication and provide interventions; every medical decision influences the patient's outcome, and inappropriate decisions result in deterioration or death. The system produces a timeline report and performance metrics benchmarked to clinical guidelines, made available online to the tutor for evaluation. In this study 21 patient-based cases were delivered in two-hour tutored online sessions.

Online access modality, the only one used in this study, via a dedicated multi-touch table or online access

Students' performance scores in each simulated case were not considered in the final analysis

examples: 21 cardiovascular, trauma, pneumological, infective, gynaecology, gastrointestinal, nephrological and hypoglycaemia cases were presented in two-hour sessions split into introduction, virtual patient-based training and debriefing

description: The program combines an intensive two-week boot camp before residency with a year of follow-on practice. article_title: Enhancing the defensibility of examiners' marks in high stake OSCEs.
citation: Shulruf Boaz, Damodaran Arvin, Jones Phil, Kennedy Sean, Mangos George, O'Sullivan Anthony J., Rhee Joel, Taylor Silas, Velan Gary, Harris Peter. (2018). Enhancing the defensibility of examiners' marks in high stake OSCEs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1112-z
title: Borderline (B) grade replacing the Borderline Pass (P-) grade in the OSCE marking schedule
description: The UNSW Medicine OSCE marking schedule previously used four grades (F, P-, P, P+) converted to scores 3, 5, 7, 9. OBM2 implementation replaced the Borderline Pass grade with a Borderline grade indicating the examiner is "unable to decide on whether the student performance was a clear pass or a clear fail related to a particular assessment criterion (item)". This allowed examiners to give an undetermined grade when appropriate, reducing examiner bias and anxiety, and simplified the marking algorithm for administrators.
requirements: Examiner training and revised assessment guides were carried out throughout the 2016 academic year before implementation
Four Faculty committees independently discussed and approved the process, with a contingency plan in place
constraints: The 5 mark remains the cut-score determined by university and faculty policies and cannot be changed by OBM2
target_learning_goals: accurate and defensible pass/fail decisions in clinical skills assessment
examples: Students and examiners welcomed the change from P- to B grades as easier to understand, and no complaints were raised across all clinical examination sites
